title: 09 — Design a Web Crawler
html:
09 — Design a Web Crawler

The one idea: a crawler is a BFS over the web graph, and the URL frontier (the queue of URLs to fetch) is the whole design: it enforces politeness (one host at a time, with delays), priority (important pages first) and freshness (recrawl what changes).

Step 1 — Scope

  • Purpose: search-engine indexing (also used for archiving, mining, monitoring).
  • 1 billion pages per month; HTML only; consider newly added and edited pages.
  • Store pages for 5 years; ignore duplicate content.

Qualities: scalability (parallel), robustness (bad HTML, traps, crashes), politeness (don't hammer a site), extensibility (new content types later).

Estimates

  • 1B ÷ 30 days ÷ 10^5 ≈ ~400 pages/s, peak ~800/s.
  • 500 KB/page → 500 TB/month → ~30 PB over 5 years.

Step 2 — High-level design

---
title: Web crawler — high-level pipeline
---
flowchart LR
    Seed["Seed URLs"] --> F["URL frontier"]
    F --> D["HTML downloader"]
    DNS["DNS resolver<br/>(cached)"] --> D
    D --> P["Content parser"]
    P --> Seen{"Content seen?<br/>(hash)"}
    Seen -->|new| CS[("Content storage")]
    Seen -->|new| LE["Link extractor"]
    LE --> UF["URL filter<br/>(type, blocklist, robots)"]
    UF --> US{"URL seen?<br/>(Bloom filter)"}
    US -->|new| F
    US -->|new| UStore[("URL storage")]
Component Job
Seed URLs Starting points — by country, by topic, or popular domains
URL frontier FIFO-ish queue of URLs to download, with politeness and priority
HTML downloader Fetches pages, respects robots.txt
DNS resolver Resolves hostnames — cached, because DNS is a known bottleneck
Content parser Validates and parses HTML
Content seen? Dedupes identical pages by hash (~30% of the web is duplicate)
Link extractor Pulls links, normalises relative → absolute
URL filter Drops unwanted types, blocklisted sites, error links
URL seen? Bloom filter / hash set to avoid re-queueing

Step 3 — Deep dive

3.1 DFS vs BFS

DFS goes too deep. BFS via a FIFO queue — but plain BFS is impolite (most links on a page point to the same host) and ignores priority.

3.2 The URL frontier

---
title: URL frontier — priority and politeness queues
---
flowchart TB
    In["URLs in"] --> Pr["Prioritiser<br/>(PageRank, traffic, freshness)"]
    Pr --> FQ1["Front queue f1<br/>(high priority)"]
    Pr --> FQn["Front queue fn<br/>(low priority)"]
    FQ1 --> Sel["Queue selector<br/>(biased to high priority)"]
    FQn --> Sel
    Sel --> Router["Queue router<br/>(host → queue mapping table)"]
    Router --> BQ1["Back queue b1<br/>host A only"]
    Router --> BQn["Back queue bn<br/>host N only"]
    BQ1 --> W1["Worker 1<br/>(delay between fetches)"]
    BQn --> Wn["Worker n"]
  • Front queues → priority. A prioritiser scores URLs; the selector picks higher-priority queues more often.
  • Back queues → politeness. Each back queue holds URLs for one host; each worker thread consumes one queue with a delay between requests. No host gets parallel hammering.
  • Freshness: recrawl based on a page's update history; prioritise important pages.
  • Storage: the frontier is huge (hundreds of millions of URLs) → mostly on disk, with in-memory buffers for enqueue/dequeue.

3.3 HTML downloader

  • robots.txt: fetch per host, cache it, obey Disallow and crawl-delay.
  • Performance: distributed crawl (hosts partitioned across servers), DNS cache, geographic locality (crawl servers near hosts), short timeouts.

3.4 Robustness

  • Consistent hashing to distribute hosts across downloader nodes.
  • Checkpoint crawl state to disk so a crash doesn't restart from zero.
  • Catch parser exceptions — one bad page must never kill a worker.
  • Validate data heavily.

3.5 Problematic content

Problem Mitigation
Duplicate content Hash (or SimHash/MinHash for near-duplicates)
Spider traps (infinite URL spaces, calendars) Max URL length, max depth per host, manual blocklist
Data noise (ads, spam) Filter out

Step 4 — Wrap-up

  • Server-side rendering: JavaScript-built pages need a headless browser to render before parsing (expensive — do it selectively).
  • Filter low-value pages early to save storage and CPU.
  • Database replication and sharding for URL and content stores.
  • Analytics on crawl rate, error rate, per-host stats.

.NET / Azure mapping

  • Downloader: HttpClient via IHttpClientFactory with SocketsHttpHandler tuned (MaxConnectionsPerServer, PooledConnectionLifetime), plus a per-host SemaphoreSlim / System.Threading.RateLimiting limiter for politeness.
  • Parsing: AngleSharp or HtmlAgilityPack.
  • Pipeline: System.Threading.Channels inside a worker; Service Bus (sessions keyed by host give per-host ordering and single-consumer semantics = politeness for free) or Storage Queues between stages.
  • Storage: Blob Storage (cool tier) for page content; Cosmos DB / Table Storage for URL metadata.
  • Scale: workers as Container Apps jobs or AKS pods scaled by queue length (KEDA).

Review checklist

  • Estimate pages/s and storage.
  • Pipeline diagram with dedupe of both content and URLs.
  • Frontier: front queues for priority, back queues for politeness.
  • robots.txt, DNS cache, timeouts.
  • Spider traps and near-duplicate detection.
